622.t: Key changes in tunes keep rhythmic playing fresh
622.s: Ashcraft explains how China Boy and New Orleans tunes modulate, giving new life to each chorus.
622.q: Well, there's something in the nature of the tunes they were playing. I mentioned China Boy, for instance. Uh, the Wolverines used to play it quite a lot because that was a standard tune they played when, uh, they were requested to play something they didn't know. Oh. If somebody, uh, it was very…

622.t: A two-chord tune Chicagoans loved playing
622.s: Ashcraft describes a tune with only two chords and how simple Chicago repertoire could be.
622.q: How, how so? Gum, for example? Oh, an example of what they did in Chicago. How simple they could be? Yes, it's a two chord tune. The second, the middle chord, uh, well, it's a lot of work. It's a verse to a tune called the Eel that Friedman is generally supposed to have written. But the, uh, we've…

732.t: Fly Me to the Moon key mix-up and relative minors
732.s: A singer asks for A and means something else; Pallo explains experience in finding the right key.
732.q: I had that case on a job that I did. A fellow came up and said I want to sing “Fly Me To the Moon.” So I said, “Well what key do you want it in?” He says, “A.” Fine. So I gave him the first note and he sang it and he said, “That’s the wrong key.” He wanted me to start on A minor seventh. Well A…

732.s: Pallo prefers flat keys; they talk about Stardust and players who cannot name their key.
732.q: And they will go to B. And guitar players love E, we say — not all guitar players — love E, A and D let’s say. I hate those keys. Not that I hate them, I’d rather play E flat, it’s more for a horn. I like E flat, I like A flat, I love D flat. But E, because I got away from

172.s: Ridgley says everyone knew who took each chorus and varied it per piece. They did not change keys on Maryland but did on The Saints.
172.q: Yeah, always. I would have to know. You knew ahead of the time when you took on Maryland who was gonna get the solo the second

623.t: Changing keys and playing in difficult keys
623.s: Discussion of musicians struggling with key changes; Smith's Janis band transposed deliberately and he explains how difficult keys alter playing.
623.q: now that's odd because even my limited experience we always played in all kinds of keys with the Conrad Janus band just for exercise we used to deliberately change keys or transpose in the middle of tunes just to you get a very different flavor out of a tune when you play it in a different key…

35.t: Long tunes, harmony and counter-melody origins
35.s: While the tape plays, they discuss hard-changed tunes, Bunk's impatience with his first band, and whether counter melodies were Bunk's originals.
35.q: yeah well he was quite impatient with his first band of the Stuyvesant because he couldn't do these so dear dear dear dear dear

647.t: Changing from Joe Robichaux's style to a modern style
647.s: He once played like Joe Robichaux but shortened his left hand and used four-part harmony for small combos.
647.q: Well, you ever heard Joe Robichaud play? Yes. I used to play like Joe Robichaud. That was, that's the man who taught. But I changed more, more modern because the fellas were telling me that the way I was playing, it was hard, with a small combo, see? For me to play like that. So when it was my…

717.t: Finding the right key for singers; difficult charts
717.s: He sets singers' keys in workshops, and Jerry Dodgion says his music is hard until learned.
717.q: pianist plays better in that key kind of a thing. And I’ll say well look it, let’s try this a half a step lower, a half a step higher. And they say wow, it feels much better.

787.t: Why the orchestration is in E rather than E flat
787.s: Broadbent describes E as bright, full and warm for strings, versus a darker E flat.
787.q: Oh yeah. Oh absolutely. E flat would be a darker sound, especially when there are strings involved, a lot of strings, and we had a lot. E becomes a bright, full, open stringed sound, but warm. E flat they’ve got a lot of stops on the — how’s that for a piano player, folks?

517.t: Joking with Marian McPartland about keys at Town Hall
517.s: At the previous night's McPartland tribute he signalled four flats for 'Centerpiece'; jazz tunes are mostly in flat keys.
517.q: Yeah, let me explain. Marian was actually joking, she said well “Centerpiece,” that’s one of the tunes that we played, that’s the tune that we played when Marian came out. It’s a Sweets’ original. Sweets Edison original. I played it with him many times before. Anybody knows it’s in the key of A…

205.t: Singers' keys, flat keys and why jazz guitarists do not use capos
205.s: Talk about playing in different keys, horn transposition, John Cephas's capo use and rock guitarists' tuning and feedback.
205.q: Oh, I love that yeah, I love that. I think there are a lot of guitar players, they love to play in those “bright” keys they call them, you know the A and the E and all that kind of stuff. But some of the newer ones, of course that read real well, they’re used to reading the tenor keys and the alto…

504.s: He transposes automatically and picks out chord changes quickly for singers.
504.q: Well I just automatically transfer it to any key. You know. And quickly pick out the chord changes and you know you had to do that with singers. Some singers just — they might sing in a different key the same song. But you know most of the singers knew what they wanted, what key they wanted to sing…

797.t: Signalling key changes to the band with fingers
797.s: Rowe asks about the hand signals for key changes; Ecklund explains flat keys suit the horns and modulations bring variety.
797.q: Well you’re right, that is the universal symbol for sharps is this and flats is that. But in fact it’s too difficult to do that, like if everyone’s standing up you can’t go like this. And nearly everything we play is either in C or in flat keys. We’re not going to play anything in D. We might play…

107.t: Why Basie played so few minor-key tunes
107.s: Minor tunes were more common in the 1940s and early 50s; they still sounded cheerful.
107.ch: Basie band: origins, sound and style
107.q: Yes, in the early 50’s and going back in the 40’s, there were several more perhaps, than we did in the 60’s and 70’s and 80’s, cause “Topsy” was one of them, what’s that thing — “Tickle Toe?”

599.t: Singing in standard keys for sidemen
599.s: He sings in standard keys so musicians can play comfortably, though range matters.
599.q: Well I’m lucky. A lot of the songs that I sing I sing in the standard key, which certainly makes them happy. I mean you play, you know a good musician can play in any key. But they’re comfortable in the keys that the songs are in. I mean if I could sing — you know it does make a difference I mean…

808.s: She knows her keys, brings written charts, and notes horn players prefer flat keys.
808.q: Oh I should hope so. Because I have a very narrow range so there’s not much room for error. We’ve got to do it in my key or we can’t do it at all.

514.t: Accompanying singers at Birdland and playing in all keys
514.s: At Birdland he backed many singers between Coltrane's quartet and Horace Silver's quintet sets, which sharpened his accompanying and transposing.
514.q: Johnny Hartman, I played with Irene Reid, I had all the singing gigs from Birdland so consequently I was always on the scene. See it would be three bands. John Coltrane Quartet, Benny Carter Trio with Harold Mabern and Ron Carter and Roy McCurdy or Bill Lee and Roy McCurdy. Then I’d take a break…

745.t: Playing for singers and different keys
745.s: Different keys are easy on bass because of finger patterns, though he has misled singers.
745.q: Yeah sometimes. But most of the time on bass it’s not a big problem because of the way the bass is set up. It’s just basically playing the same finger patterns but moving your hand to a different area. It’s not like you have to play the black keys or you know, whatever they go through – madness…

595.t: Playing in odd keys: Ray Brown and Lester Young
595.s: Pell explains three flats, tells of Ray Brown's E-blues trap, and says Lester Young deliberately changed keys to unsettle horn players.
595.ch: Lester Young and the Prez Conference
595.q: It’s in three flats because down is flats and if you are going to play in four sharps, like Lester, or seven sharps like Lester, he always did that kind of number, so you’d figure in all the sharps and then flat the fifth. And there’s a story about Ray Brown. We were doing a show one day and they…

785.t: The half-step modulation and thinking of keys as feelings
785.s: The video was a sound test in the car; the bassist did not know of the modulation. Sands thinks of keys as gestures and feelings.
785.q: Probably not. I mean this was — the recording that we did, I mean that video was actually just purely just us testing the sound of us, so it wasn’t like a pre-thought piece that we were going to play for the show, we just ended up, it was just in the car while we were driving there and so well…

451.t: The feeling of keys and open strings
451.s: Key choice, open strings, Chelsea Bridge in D-flat.
451.q: Well, that’s interesting, yeah. Well, occasionally, I’ll play it, something in a key where I can use the open strings on the guitar, and generally, that would mean something with sharps in it like E major or A major. I’ve written that thing called Careful is in A major, and it has a, based on a…

227.t: Walking through Central Park and the modulations
227.s: Mandel recalls working out the ending while walking through Central Park, and Kirchner traces the chart's modulations.
227.ch: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
227.q: I remember one thing about that chart, I spent a lot of time on it, but I figured out the whole last part of it when I was walking through Central Park, after getting off work. In those days, in 1947 you could walk through Central Park at four or five in the morning and I figured that whole ending…

168.t: Passing tones and the pop tunes that opened up the harmony
168.s: Half his work was bowed solos and humming; passing tones replaced plain triads, helped by ballads like The Man I Love and Tenderly.
168.ch: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
168.q: What have you, passing tones. Passing tones, what would you say, elaborate upon more passing tones instead of straight triads and what have you.

169.t: 'Mop-Mop', 'I Got Rhythm' and harmony after 'How High the Moon'
169.s: New lines on old changes, and the success of 'How High the Moon' changing harmony.
169.ch: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
169.q: Well, I don't know whether Charlie played that particular thing. I don't even know whether Hawk put it out. All I know is that when I came to New York they were playing it. So I don't know who wrote it, or who thought about the idea. But I know that everybody was playing it. I thought that it…

237.s: Goodwin says Jesse Stone began writing only chord symbols for soloists in the early thirties, making players chord-conscious.
237.q: My first recognition of a change in solos was -- say trombone, trumpet or saxophone or whatever, woodwind or brass, I noticed a trend back in the early '30s where they began to insert chords and make the musician other than guitar or banjo or piano, they were more chord conscious you know.

124.t: Choosing a song's key; song pluggers and sheet music
124.s: Songs are published in the key that fits the average singer, and five-and-ten song demonstrators played them in any key.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: The three songs are the keys what -- sometime we just find -- When you're writing a song, we just pick out a song according to how -- whatever the range of the song is. 78.t: Three-minute records and abrupt key changes
78.s: To fit the three-minute limit arrangers cut endings and modulated abruptly; Horace still uses such key jumps in his small combo.
78.ch: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
78.q: Right. Right. And they would watch that clock. That second hand would be going like mad, you know. And a lot of times they'd do this. We'd run over.
